_comment: What this stack's machines must DO, declared by the stack (#503).
tools/conformance/functional.sh reads this file and nothing else decides
what it asserts: an assertion table living in the harness would be 'what
somebody thought to check', which is the criticism examples/stacks exists
to answer for the configurations themselves.
Every one of the four families must appear. A family this stack cannot
offer is written as {"skip": "<reason>"} and the run stays exit 0 while
naming the bound out loud — a check that skips in silence is worse than
an absent one. A family that is simply missing is a FAIL, because 'this
stack declares nothing about its firewall' is a finding, not a default.
Machine names are the names the provider's own API publishes, resolved
through /_feint/state to the machine the runtime holds. Ports are the
ports the stack's own security groups name: every value here is readable
in main.tf beside the rule that makes it true.
_running_state: What this provider calls a machine that is up, which is machine.Binding's
RunningState and a per-pack fact rather than a shared word: the three packs
spell the failed one 'stopped', 'stopped' and 'error'. Declared here so a
fourth pack states its own instead of inheriting a guess.

_why: The web tier serves 443, which is the port scaleway_instance_security_group.web
opens, from an installed systemd unit rather than a transient one.
restart names the machine the harness stops and starts again through the
provider's API. It is poweroff+poweron and not the reboot action, and that
is a measurement rather than a preference: on 2026-08-27 a reboot answered
success, left the container's pid and uptime untouched and a transient
marker unit still active: nothing restarted, so an assertion resting on it
would be a control that cannot fail. Filed as #547.
Both halves on one machine, in one pass: the app tier listens on 8080 and
on 9090, its group opens 8080 to the web block and names 9090 nowhere, and
both probes leave the same web machine. So the only thing that differs
between the two verdicts is the rule.
Across two subnets on purpose. Within one subnet the sender's permissive
egress outranks the receiver's ingress default (docs/limits.md, measured
again here on 2026-08-27: web-0 reached web-1 on a port no rule opens, and
so did app-worker-b), so a closure probed from a neighbour would measure
nothing. Traffic entering through the router port carries no sender rule,
and the receiver's policy holds.
The liveness of both ports is proved from inside the target before either
verdict is drawn, which is what tells a refusal from a dead service.

control_source.skip: no machine of this stack sits outside 10.30.1.0/24 and on a network peered with the app tier's. The bastion is in the management VPC, so a refusal from it would be isolation rather than the rule, and an app worker is the target's own neighbour, which the documented same-subnet bound lets through whatever the group says (measured 2026-08-27: app-worker-b reached app-worker-a on 8080). The source restriction is measured on the Outscale stack instead, whose two public subnets give a source the rule does not name.

_why: reaches: two machines of one private network, on the port their shared
group opens.
isolated: platform-admin belongs to the management VPC and the web network
to the workload one, so nothing peers them. The port is 22, which the
bastion's group opens to 0.0.0.0/0 — a refusal there cannot be the rule.
Gated on capabilities.isolation: the bridge mode does not deliver it and
says so, and the harness skips rather than asserting what nobody promised.

balancer.skip: the Scaleway pack does not hand its load balancers to the runtime: enforced.balancing names outscale alone (#481), and a balancer here records its configuration and forwards nothing (docs/limits.md). The harness re-reads that declaration at run time rather than trusting this line, so the day the pack wires it, this skip stops being taken.
